title: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
shortTitle: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service
summary: A Windows service is a background process started by the Service Control Manager, and its configuration lives in the registry, primarily under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services. Each service key holds an ImagePath that names the executable, plus optional failure recovery commands, a start type that decides whether it loads at boot, and an ObjectName that decides which account the process runs as. An attacker with administrative rights can add a new service, repoint an existing ImagePath, or write the registry values directly; services are also a delivery route for kernel drivers, where a .sys file is registered and loaded so it runs in kernel mode and can act as a rootkit or support a vulnerable-driver attack. The defensive value of this technique is that registering a service requires high privilege, while the resulting process usually runs as SYSTEM, so a single change can escalate rights as well as persist. Detection leans on configuration-change evidence, such as registry value set events and service creation records, correlated with a start event. Windows Security 4688 process creation showing services.exe as the parent of an unexpected binary is the classic pairing. Service names borrowed from real vendors, image paths in user-writable directories, and services deliberately hidden from enumeration by permission changes all raise the score.

beginner.definition: A Windows service is a program that Windows starts by itself, usually when the computer boots, and then keeps running in the background. The settings for each service are stored in a database called the registry. This technique is when an attacker adds a new service or changes an existing one to run their own program.
beginner.whyItMatters: A malicious service starts again at every boot, so the attacker keeps access without doing anything else. Services normally run as SYSTEM, the most powerful local account, so the attacker gains far more control than they started with. It is also a common way to load a malicious driver deep inside Windows. Spotting it early is therefore very important.
howItWorks: The attacker first copies their program, or a driver file, onto the disk of the victim machine.
They then create a service entry that points at that file, often using the built-in sc command.
The entry also records the start type, which decides whether the service loads at boot.
An existing service can be edited instead, so a trusted name quietly runs a different program.
Driver services are loaded into the kernel, where they can hide files and processes from the user.
Windows then starts the service, usually as SYSTEM, every time the machine boots.
beginner.example: Think of a hotel that keeps a maintenance book behind the front desk. Each entry says which room to service each morning. Someone adds an entry naming a storeroom that only they use, and notes that the work should be done by the senior manager. Every morning the manager unlocks that storeroom on schedule, and no guest ever sees it happen.
takeaways: Service settings live in the registry, so registry change logs are a key detection source.
A new service that starts a program from a temporary or user folder deserves a close look.
The same mechanism can load a malicious driver, which is far harder to see from user space.

objectives: Explain how the Service Control Manager starts services on Windows.
Describe where service configuration is stored and which values matter most.
Explain how a service can be used to escalate privileges to SYSTEM.
Explain how services are abused to load malicious or vulnerable drivers.
Identify process creation and registry events that reveal a suspicious service.
